items.prompt: The original route wrote body as { ingredients: unknown; ... }. A client posts the JSON literal null. What did the assertion do about it?
items.answer: Nothing: an assertion only tells the compiler how to type the value
distractors: It threw a TypeError, because null does not match the asserted shape
It converted null into an empty object whose fields were all undefined
Nothing in the handler, because Next.js rejected the null body first
items.explanation: A TypeScript assertion does not inspect the value. The revised parser accepts unknown, and its record() guard is what rejects null at runtime before returning typed values.

items.prompt: A request arrives with servings as the string "2". How many paid provider calls does generateRecipeResponse make?
items.answer: Zero: input parsing runs before the retry loop, and the route returns 400
distractors: One: the provider is asked once, and then its output fails validation
Two: both attempts run, because the retry loop catches every error
One: the string "2" is coerced to the number 2 and generation succeeds
items.explanation: parseGenerationInput runs before the retry loop. Placing parsing there means retrying can never turn invalid input into a paid request - correctness and cost control at once.

items.prompt: Which normalisation does the parser perform on accepted values?
items.answer: It only trims text; a numeric string like "2" is rejected, not converted
distractors: It trims text and parses numeric strings such as "2" into real numbers
It lowercases every string so that later comparisons are case-insensitive
None at all: every value is returned exactly as it was received
items.explanation: text() returns the trimmed value; number() rejects strings, NaN and Infinity, so numbers must already be finite numbers.

items.prompt: A request lists ingredients [" Rice", "rice "]. What is the response?
items.answer: 400 'Ingredients must be distinct.', after trimming and lowercasing both
distractors: 200, because the two raw strings differ in their whitespace and case
200 with a single rice ingredient, after silent deduplication
400 'Ingredient must be non-empty text', because of the whitespace
items.explanation: text() trims both, then the Set comparison uses lowercased values: two spellings of one ingredient are rejected, not silently merged.

items.prompt: A request includes an extra field injected: "ignored". Does it reach the provider?
items.answer: No: the parser builds a new object from the named fields only
distractors: Yes: unknown fields pass through to the provider untouched
No: the request is rejected with a 400 for unexpected fields
Yes, but parseRecipes strips it from the provider's output later
items.explanation: Constructing the output from named fields drops anything else by construction, and the boundary test asserts the provider saw exactly the normalized input.

items.prompt: The request asks for 30 minutes and 2 servings. The provider returns three well-formed recipes, one taking 45 minutes. What happens?
items.answer: parseRecipes throws, so that attempt fails and the orchestrator may retry
distractors: The 45-minute recipe is dropped, and the other two recipes are returned
All three are returned, because each recipe is individually well-formed
The 45-minute recipe's time is clamped to 30 minutes before it is returned
items.explanation: parseRecipes throws 'Recipes must respect the requested time and servings.' Cross-field rules only run when the caller passes the accepted input; they check fit, not just shape.

items.prompt: The provider returns unparseable output twice in a row. What does the browser receive?
items.answer: A 500 with a generic 'Couldn't generate recipes' message and no details
distractors: A 500 whose body contains the parser's specific error message
A 502 that includes the raw provider response body to help with debugging
A 200 with an empty recipes array, after both attempts are spent
items.explanation: Model output is nondeterministic, so one retry may help; after two failures the response stays generic - provider details are never copied into the response.

items.prompt: Saved history contains four entries, two of them malformed. What does reading it return, and is storage changed?
items.answer: The two valid entries, and the stored string is not rewritten by the read
distractors: An empty list, because one bad entry invalidates the whole collection
The two valid entries, and storage is rewritten on the spot without the bad ones
All four entries, with the two malformed ones flagged as corrupt
items.explanation: Bad entries are dropped individually. History is a collection of independent records, so partial recovery is useful - and reads must not perform destructive cleanup.

items.prompt: Why does a provider response with one bad recipe fail entirely, while history with one bad entry recovers partially?
items.answer: A response is one new collection with one contract; history is user-owned records
distractors: A bad provider response is cheaper to retry than a history read is to redo
localStorage cannot throw, so a full failure there is impossible anyway
It is an arbitrary style choice between throwing and catching made in each module
items.explanation: A provider response must satisfy the whole contract; history is independent records the user owns, so dropping only the bad one is useful. The policy difference comes from ownership and user expectations, not from a preference for exceptions.

items.prompt: A vegan request returns recipes containing butter marked isFromUser: true. Does the parser catch it?
items.answer: No: it checks shape and arithmetic, not diet or isFromUser truth
distractors: Yes: dietary preferences are cross-checked against ingredient names
Yes: isFromUser ingredients are matched against the request list
Only when allowMissingOne is false, which turns on strict matching
items.explanation: It verifies shape and arithmetic, not truth: neither dietary compliance nor that isFromUser ingredients appear in the user's list is checked. Do not turn a successful parser result into a stronger product claim than its code supports.

items.prompt: A crafted share link decodes to {"title":"x"}. What happens on the shared-recipe page?
items.answer: It is cast to Recipe unvalidated, so rendering crashes on ingredients.map
distractors: decodeRecipe returns null, and the page shows a 'recipe not found' message
parseRecipe rejects it inside decodeRecipe, and the page redirects home
The missing fields default to empty arrays, and the page renders anyway
items.explanation: decodeRecipe returns JSON.parse(...) as Recipe with no validation, so rendering crashes at recipe.ingredients.map. The fix wraps the parse in parseRecipe inside the existing try, so the catch returns null for invalid links.

items.prompt: Why does the in-memory rate limiter limit honest users but not attackers?
items.answer: It keys on the client-set x-forwarded-for header, which attackers rotate
distractors: It counts requests per minute but resets the count on every successful call
It only applies to GET requests, while recipe generation is sent as a POST
It limits by API key, and attackers simply send requests without any key
items.explanation: The key is the client-controlled x-forwarded-for header, so an attacker rotates values; the Map also never evicts and is per-instance on serverless. Rated Medium because each bypassed request can cost a paid provider call.

items.front: Name the three contracts the parser distinguishes (request contract in lib/validation.ts:39-67) and what each checks.
items.back: Request: 2-20 distinct ingredient strings, a time limit of 15/30/45/60, 1-6 whole servings, supported dietary options, skill choice, real boolean. Recipe: nested objects, positive finite amounts, bounded text, consecutive step order. Collection: exactly three distinct ids, time/servings/missing-ingredient consistent with the accepted request.

items.front: The four parser primitives in lib/validation.ts:10-37 - what does each accept?
items.back: record: plain objects (not null, arrays, primitives). text: non-blank strings up to a trimmed maximum, returns the trimmed value. number: finite numbers in [min, max], optionally integers. list: arrays with length in [min, max].

items.front: Recipe ids are checked distinct only within a batch (lib/validation.ts:109). Why is that a bug for favourites, and where is the clean fix?
items.back: Favourites are keyed by id globally, so two batches can reuse an id and toggling one recipe un-favourites another. Fix on the server right after parseRecipes succeeds in lib/generation.ts: replace each id with crypto.randomUUID() so every consumer sees globally unique ids.

items.front: Finding 5: lib/generation.ts:24-26 catches every provider/parse error silently. What is the operability cost, and what should a fix add without leaking details?
items.back: A missing API key is indistinguishable from bad output. Log an internal event with a correlation id, attempt number and a bounded category (parse_failure, transport_failure) while keeping the public response generic - test that a distinctive private message is absent from the response.
